posts.title: Pseudobulk First for Single-Cell Differential Expression
posts.excerpt: Why sample-level pseudobulk is usually the cleanest default for replicated single-cell differential expression.

content.text: For condition-level differential expression in single-cell RNA-seq, the biological replicate is the donor, animal, well, organoid, or sample. Cells are nested measurements inside that replicate. Treating every cell as independent can make p-values look stronger than the biological evidence really is.

Pseudobulk keeps the inference aligned with the experiment. After QC and annotation, raw counts are summed for each sample-by-cell-type pair. Each cell type then becomes a familiar bulk RNA-seq problem where edgeR or DESeq2 can model counts, covariates, batches, and contrasts directly.

rows: Needs raw counts and real biological replicates
Stable lab workflows and familiar reports
Still depends on filtering and correct design
More tuning and compute; not usually the default

content.text: Keep raw integer counts in a dedicated layer, finish cell annotation before testing, and check that every condition has enough biological replication. Weak cell types should be filtered before interpretation, not explained away after the model.

Aggregate raw counts, align sample metadata, filter low-information genes, then run edgeR quasi-likelihood or DESeq2 with the design formula that matches the study. Useful covariates often include batch, donor, sex, time point, exposure group, or sequencing run.

Interpret the result above the gene-list level. In exposure biology, the strongest stories usually come from affected programs: oxidative stress, xenobiotic metabolism, inflammation, mitochondrial function, unfolded protein response, or cell-cycle shifts in specific populations.

rows: Python: `pb = dc.pp.pseudobulk(adata, sample_col='sample', groups_col='cell_type', layer='counts', mode='sum')`
R: `fit <- glmQLFit(y, design); res <- glmQLFTest(fit, coef='conditionexposed')`

items: Use the sample or donor as the unit of inference.
Sum raw counts by sample and cell type.
Filter weak cell types before making biological claims.
Use edgeR or DESeq2 as the primary model.
Translate DE into pathways or regulator activity.

posts.title: A Design-First Strategy for Multi-Omics Integration
posts.excerpt: A short decision guide for choosing MOFA+, DIABLO, WNN, or MultiVI from the study design.

content.text: Multi-omics integration should start with the study design, not with the software. The key questions are simple: are modalities measured on the same samples, the same cells, or partly missing across batches? Is the goal discovery, prediction, clustering, imputation, or mechanism?

Once those constraints are clear, method choice becomes easier. MOFA+ is useful for unsupervised factor discovery in matched datasets. DIABLO is better when labels are known and the goal is a compact predictive signature. WNN is a strong default for paired multimodal single-cell clustering. MultiVI is useful when paired and unpaired RNA/ATAC data need one latent space.

rows: Unsupervised factors across matched omics layers
Not a classifier; covariate checks still matter
Best for graph analysis, not every integration task
More compute and model discipline required

content.text: Run unimodal QC first: PCA or UMAP per modality, sample clustering, missingness summaries, batch diagnostics, and basic differential checks. Integration should solve a defined problem, not hide a weak assay or an unresolved batch effect.

For matched bulk studies, normalize each view appropriately and check whether latent factors track biology rather than run date. For supervised models, reserve validation data. For single-cell multimodal data, ask whether integration improves annotation and interpretation, not just whether the embedding looks smooth.

rows: R: `MOFAobject <- create_mofa(list(rna=rna, prot=prot, metab=metab)); MOFAobject <- run_mofa(MOFAobject)`

items: Choose the method from data geometry and question.
Use MOFA+ for matched unsupervised factor discovery.
Use DIABLO for supervised signatures tied to an outcome.
Use WNN for paired multimodal single-cell clustering.
Use MultiVI when missing RNA/ATAC modalities matter.

posts.title: Building a Reproducible Omics Pipeline That Survives Review
posts.excerpt: A compact blueprint for moving an omics analysis from notebook to citable workflow.

content.text: A notebook that works on one machine is not yet a reproducible pipeline. A review-ready analysis needs explicit inputs, explicit outputs, locked software, and a way to rerun the workflow on another machine without guessing.

The goal is not to over-engineer every project. The goal is to make the analysis portable enough that collaborators, reviewers, and future lab members can regenerate the main results from a stable command and documented environment.

rows: Paper pipelines and analysis-first lab projects
The same environment must rebuild later
CI, local development, or HPC deployment

content.text: Start with a notebook that already works. Move repeated logic into scripts. Put those scripts behind Snakemake or Nextflow rules. Lock the environment. Add a small test dataset. Run that test in CI. Tag a stable release and archive it with a DOI.

Snakemake is often the lowest-friction choice for a lab analysis becoming a paper workflow. Nextflow is stronger when the pipeline needs to run across clusters, cloud systems, or many users. The best choice is the one your team can maintain.

Testing should be small and automatic. A miniature dataset that finishes quickly is enough to catch broken paths, changed dependencies, and accidental output changes before they reach a manuscript analysis.

rows: GitHub plus Zenodo: tag a release, archive it, and cite the DOI

items: Move repeated notebook logic into scripts.
Use one workflow engine and one environment strategy.
Lock environments before the project becomes hard to rebuild.
Add a tiny end-to-end test dataset.
Tag stable releases and archive them with a DOI.
